title: Doctrine of Promissory Estoppel against the State (Motilal Padampat Sugar Mills)

content.overview: Promissory estoppel prevents a public authority from resiling from a clear promise or representation where the promisee has altered position in reliance on it, and where it would be inequitable to allow the authority to go back on the promise. Against the State, the doctrine is applied as a rule of equity and fairness, subject to statutory power and overriding public interest.
content.glance: Identify a clear promise or representation by the authority, reliance and change of position by the promisee, inequity if the promise is withdrawn, and any public-interest or ultra vires limit on enforcement.
content.study:
Core rule: where a public authority makes a clear and unequivocal promise or representation intending that it should be acted upon, and the promisee does act upon it to their detriment or by altering position, the authority may be estopped from resiling if it would be inequitable to allow withdrawal.

Ingredients: (1) a clear promise or representation by the authority; (2) intention or reasonable expectation that it will be acted upon; (3) reliance by the promisee; (4) alteration of position; and (5) inequity in permitting the authority to go back on the promise.

Against the State: Indian law recognises that promissory estoppel can operate against the Government. The State is not exempt merely because it is the State. However, the doctrine cannot compel an ultra vires act, nor can it freeze the State's power to change policy where overriding public interest so requires and fairness is observed.

Relationship to legitimate expectation: Both doctrines protect reliance on governmental conduct. Promissory estoppel is rooted in equity and focuses on a specific promise and detrimental reliance. Legitimate expectation is a public-law fairness doctrine that may arise from promise, practice or policy and is primarily procedural. Analyse them separately when both are pleaded.

Limits: No estoppel from an illegal promise; no estoppel that disables the State from performing a statutory duty; public interest may justify departure in appropriate cases. Mere negotiations or tentative statements do not amount to a clear promise.

Current-law framing: Ground the analysis in the Constitution and the specific statute or executive power under which the promise was made. Do not treat the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 as the source of promissory estoppel; evidence provisions apply only when proof issues arise.

sections.heading: Meaning and Purpose
sections.body: Promissory estoppel is an equitable doctrine that holds a promisor to a clear promise where the promisee has relied upon it and altered position. Against the State, its purpose is to secure fairness and prevent the Government from going back on representations that have induced legitimate reliance, within the limits of law and public interest.

sections.heading: Ingredients of the Doctrine
sections.body: Establish a clear and unequivocal promise or representation by the authority; reliance by the promisee; alteration of position; and inequity if the authority is allowed to resile. Vague, provisional or illegal statements do not satisfy the first ingredient.

sections.heading: Operation Against the State
sections.body: The doctrine applies to governmental promises. The State cannot claim a general immunity from estoppel. At the same time, estoppel cannot compel the State to act outside its statutory power or to abandon a lawful policy change required by overriding public interest, provided fairness is respected.

sections.heading: Limits: Ultra Vires and Public Interest
sections.body: An illegal or ultra vires promise cannot be enforced through estoppel. Where the State demonstrates overriding public interest for withdrawing a promise, courts examine whether departure is justified and whether any transitional fairness was afforded. Estoppel is not a tool to freeze executive policy permanently.

sections.heading: Remedies
sections.body: Relief may include holding the authority to the promise, quashing a contradictory decision, or moulding equitable relief short of specific enforcement where public interest or statutory limits intervene. The precise remedy depends on the nature of the promise and the record.

examples.title: Clear incentive promise and reliance
examples.body: A government circular promises a tax holiday to industries that set up units in a notified area by a stated date. An industrialist invests substantially in reliance on the circular. The State then withdraws the holiday for that class. The issue is whether promissory estoppel restrains withdrawal on those facts.

examples.title: Tentative negotiation, not a promise
examples.body: Officials discuss possible concessions in correspondence marked provisional and subject to cabinet approval. No formal assurance is issued. The claimant invests anyway. The analysis must test whether a clear promise existed at all.

examples.title: Ultra vires assurance
examples.body: An officer promises a benefit that the governing statute does not authorise. The claimant relies on the promise. Estoppel cannot compel the State to act outside its statutory power.

hypotheticals.question: Does every governmental assurance create promissory estoppel?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. Require a clear promise, reliance, alteration of position and inequity. Tentative, conditional or illegal statements do not found estoppel. Even a clear promise may yield to overriding public interest or statutory limits.

hypotheticals.question: How does promissory estoppel differ from legitimate expectation on the same facts?
hypotheticals.analysis: Promissory estoppel focuses on a specific promise and detrimental reliance in equity. Legitimate expectation is a public-law fairness doctrine that may arise from promise, practice or policy and is primarily procedural. Plead and analyse them as distinct grounds.

distinctions.title: Promissory estoppel vs legitimate expectation
distinctions.left: Promissory estoppel is an equitable doctrine centred on a clear promise and detrimental reliance.
distinctions.right: Legitimate expectation is a public-law fairness doctrine arising from promise, practice or policy.

rows.left: Clear promise + reliance + change of position.
rows.right: Representation, practice or published policy generating expectation.

rows.left: Holding the promisor to the promise where inequitable to resile.
rows.right: Primarily procedural hearing before departure; limited substantive protection.

distinctions.title: Promissory estoppel vs concluded contract
distinctions.left: Estoppel may operate even without a concluded formal contract if the ingredients are met.
distinctions.right: A contract creates mutual legal obligations under the law of contract.

rows.left: Promise, reliance and inequity — not necessarily offer, acceptance and consideration in the contractual sense.
rows.right: Requires the elements of a valid contract under the governing law.

rows.left: Subject to ultra vires and public-interest limits.
rows.right: Also subject to constitutional and statutory capacity of the State to contract.

misconceptions.trap: The Government is never bound by its promises.
misconceptions.correction: Promissory estoppel can operate against the State; there is no general immunity.

misconceptions.trap: Any informal assurance creates an enforceable estoppel.
misconceptions.correction: The promise must be clear and unequivocal; provisional or illegal statements do not suffice.

misconceptions.trap: Estoppel can compel an ultra vires act.
misconceptions.correction: No estoppel can force the State to act outside its statutory power.

cases.name: Union of India v Indo-Afghan Agencies Ltd
cases.facts: Exporters acted on an export-promotion scheme under which the Government had held out certain import entitlements.
cases.issue: Whether the Government could resile from the representations in the scheme after exporters had acted upon them.
cases.ratioDecidendi: The Court recognised that the Government may be bound by its representations where persons have acted on them, and that equity may prevent resiling in appropriate cases.
cases.holding: The Court applied promissory estoppel principles to the governmental representation under challenge.
cases.relevance: Foundational authority on promissory estoppel against the Government.

cases.name: Motilal Padampat Sugar Mills Co Ltd v State of Uttar Pradesh
cases.facts: An industrial unit was set up in reliance on a governmental assurance of sales-tax exemption for a stated period.
cases.issue: Whether the State could withdraw the exemption contrary to its assurance after the promisee had altered position.
cases.ratioDecidendi: The Court held that promissory estoppel can bind the Government; consideration in the strict contractual sense is not required; the doctrine is based on equity and prevents resiling where it would be inequitable.
cases.holding: The State was held bound by the assurance on the facts of reliance and change of position.
cases.relevance: Leading modern authority on promissory estoppel against the State; named in the topic title.

cases.name: Kasinka Trading v Union of India
cases.facts: The claimants relied on a customs notification conferring exemption; the exemption was later withdrawn.
cases.issue: Whether promissory estoppel prevented the Government from withdrawing the exemption notification.
cases.ratioDecidendi: The Court examined the limits of promissory estoppel, including the Government's power to change policy in public interest and the need for a clear promise founding the estoppel claim.
cases.holding: The Court applied those limits to the withdrawal of the exemption under challenge.
cases.relevance: Authority on public-interest limits and the need for a clear foundation for estoppel against the State.

questionsAndAnswers.question: How should a promissory-estoppel challenge against the State be analysed?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: I. Identify the clear promise or representation. II. Establish reliance and alteration of position. III. Assess inequity if the State resiles. IV. Test ultra vires and overriding public-interest limits. V. Identify the appropriate equitable or public-law remedy.

questionsAndAnswers.question: What should written submissions on promissory estoppel against the State contain?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: Set out the promise and the acts of reliance; establish each ingredient; answer the State's public-interest or ultra vires defence; distinguish legitimate expectation if also pleaded; and seek only the relief supported by equity and the governing law.
